body:
This page collects instructions for the body — how to sit, stand, breathe, count and move — as they are written in books the library holds. The sources run from Ge Hong’s Baopuzi (c. 320) and a fourth-century Greek papyrus to a Marathi pole-gymnastics manual of 1922, in Chinese, Sanskrit, Hindi, Tibetan, Greek, Latin, Arabic, French and English.

Chinese and Indian authors wrote dedicated manuals: named postures with counts, hours and seasons, often with a picture. Greek and Latin authors put the same kind of instruction into other genres: the lives of philosophers, liturgies, magical rites, regimens for scholars and fencing treatises. The sections below follow that division. Each entry quotes the original and gives the Source Library translation beside it, with a link to the page.

Each entry gives the source text as printed, then the Source Library translation. Numbers in red are the counts the text itself gives. Every entry links to its page.

A year of exercises 二十四氣導引

Wang Qi and Wang Siyi, Sancai tuhui, juan 74 · Nanjing, 1609

The Chinese year has twenty-four solar terms, one every fifteen days. This chapter gives a seated exercise for each, to be done before dawn in the hours of the Ox and Tiger, one to five in the morning. Each entry names the meridian the season governs, the movement, the count, and the ailments it treats. The formula at the end is always the same: click the teeth, breathe out the old and in the new, swallow the saliva. Each woodcut links to its page; open “The text” for the Chinese and the translation.

  1. 立春 Start of Spring 3–5
    The text

    每日子丑時疊手按腔轉身抅頸左右聳引各三五度叩齒吐納漱咽

    In the hours of the Rat and the Ox, fold the hands and press the ribcage; turn the body and clasp the neck, drawing up left and right, three to five times each. Click the teeth; breathe out the old and in the new; rinse and swallow.

    Sancai tuhui, juan 74, p. 4

  2. 雨水 Rain Water 3–5
    The text

    每日子丑時疊手按脛抅頸轉身左右偏引各三五度叩齒吐納漱咽

    In the hours of the Rat and the Ox, fold the hands and press the shins; clasp the neck and turn the body, drawing to one side, left and right, three to five times each. Click the teeth; breathe; rinse and swallow.

    Sancai tuhui, juan 74, p. 5

  3. 驚蟄 Waking of Insects 36
    The text

    每日丑寅時握固轉頸及肘後向頓掣叩齒六六吐納漱咽三三

    In the hours of the Ox and the Tiger, clench the fists firmly. Turn the neck and look back toward the elbows, pulling and jerking. Click the teeth thirty-six times; breathe; rinse and swallow nine.

    Sancai tuhui, juan 74, p. 6

  4. 春分 Spring Equinox 6–7
    The text

    每日丑寅時伸手廻頭左右挽引各六七度叩齒六六吐納漱咽三三

    Extend the hands and turn the head, pulling and stretching left and right, six or seven times each. Click the teeth thirty-six times; breathe; rinse and swallow nine.

    Sancai tuhui, juan 74, p. 7

  5. 清明 Pure Brightness 7–8
    The text

    每日丑寅時正坐撫手左右如引硬弓各七八度叩齒納清吐濁咽液各三

    Sit upright and move the hands left and right as if drawing a stiff bow, seven or eight times each side. Click the teeth; inhale the clear and exhale the turbid; swallow saliva three times each.

    Sancai tuhui, juan 74, p. 8

  6. 穀雨 Grain Rain 5–7
    The text

    每日丑寅時平坐撚手左右舉托移臂左右掩乳各五七度叩齒吐納咽漱

    Sit level. Twist the hands and raise them left and right as if supporting a great weight; move the arms to cover the chest left and right, five to seven times each. Click the teeth; breathe; swallow and rinse.

    Sancai tuhui, juan 74, p. 9

  7. 立夏 Start of Summer 5–7
    The text

    每日寅卯時閉息瞑目反換兩手抑挈兩膝各五七度叩齒吐納咽液

    In the hours of the Tiger and the Hare, hold the breath and close the eyes. Alternately switch the hands to press down and pull up on both knees, five to seven times each side. Click the teeth; breathe; swallow.

    Sancai tuhui, juan 74, p. 10

  8. 小滿 Grain Full 3–5
    The text

    每日寅卯時正坐一手舉托一手拄按左右各三五度叩齒吐納咽液

    Sit upright. Raise one hand as if supporting a weight while the other presses firmly down; left and right, three to five times each. Click the teeth; breathe; swallow.

    Sancai tuhui, juan 74, p. 11

  9. 芒種 Grain in Ear 5–6
    The text

    每日寅卯時正立仰身兩手上托左右力舉各五六度定息叩齒吐納咽液

    Stand upright and arch the body back. Push both hands upward, lifting with strength left and right, five or six times each. Settle the breath; click the teeth; breathe; swallow.

    Sancai tuhui, juan 74, p. 12

  10. 夏至 Summer Solstice 5–7
    The text

    每日寅卯時跪坐伸手叉指屈腳換踏左右各五七

    Kneel and sit. Extend the hands and interlace the fingers; bend a foot and tread with each in turn, left and right, five to seven times.

    Sancai tuhui, juan 74, p. 13

  11. 小暑 Minor Heat 3–5
    The text

    每日丑寅時兩手踞屈壓一足直伸一足用力掣三五度叩齒吐納咽液

    Support yourself on both hands in a crouch; press one leg bent while the other is stretched straight, pulling with force, three to five times. Click the teeth; breathe; swallow.

    Sancai tuhui, juan 74, p. 14

  12. 大暑 Major Heat 3–5
    The text

    每日丑寅時雙拳踞地返首肩引作虎眎左右各三五度叩齒吐納咽液

    Crouch with both fists on the ground. Turn the head back over the shoulder and make the tiger’s stare, left and right, three to five times each. Click the teeth; breathe; swallow.

    Sancai tuhui, juan 74, p. 15

  13. 立秋 Start of Autumn 7–8
    The text

    每日丑寅時正坐兩手托縮體閉息聳身上踴凡七八度叩齒吐納咽潄

    Sit upright. Both hands support; draw the body in, hold the breath, and spring the body upward, seven or eight times in all. Click the teeth; breathe; swallow and rinse.

    Sancai tuhui, juan 74, p. 16

  14. 處暑 End of Heat 5–7
    The text

    每日丑寅時正坐轉頭左右舉引就返兩手搥背之上各五七度叩齒吐納咽液

    Sit upright and turn the head; raise and draw left and right, then reach both hands back and pound the upper back, five to seven times each. Click the teeth; breathe; swallow.

    Sancai tuhui, juan 74, p. 17

  15. 白露 White Dew —
    The text

    每日丑寅時正坐兩手…

    Sit upright, both hands … (the rest of the line is worn on this leaf).

    Sancai tuhui, juan 74, p. 18

  16. 秋分 Autumn Equinox 3–5
    The text

    每日丑寅時盤足而坐兩手掩耳左右返側各三五度叩齒吐納咽液

    Sit with the legs crossed. Cover both ears with the hands and turn over to each side, left and right, three to five times each. Click the teeth; breathe; swallow.

    Sancai tuhui, juan 74, p. 19

  17. 寒露 Cold Dew 3–5
    The text

    每日丑寅時正坐舉兩臂踴身上下托左右各三五度叩齒吐納咽液

    Sit upright and raise both arms. Spring the body up and down, pressing out left and right, three to five times each. Click the teeth; breathe; swallow.

    Sancai tuhui, juan 74, p. 20

  18. 霜降 Frost’s Descent 5–7
    The text

    每日丑寅時平坐紓兩手攀兩足用膝間力縱而復収五七度叩齒吐納咽液

    Sit level and extend both hands to grasp both feet. Using the strength between the knees, let the body out and draw it back, five to seven times. Click the teeth; breathe; swallow.

    Sancai tuhui, juan 74, p. 21

  19. 立冬 Start of Winter 3–5
    The text

    每日丑寅時正坐拘頸左右顧兩手左右托各三五度吐納叩齒咽液

    Sit upright and clasp the back of the neck, looking left and right; support and push with both hands left and right, three to five times each. Breathe; click the teeth; swallow.

    Sancai tuhui, juan 74, p. 22

  20. 小雪 Minor Snow 3–5
    The text

    每日丑寅時正坐一手按膝一手挽肘左右爭力各三五度吐納叩齒咽液

    Sit upright. Press one hand on the knee while the other pulls the opposite elbow; strive against each other, left and right, three to five times each. Breathe; click the teeth; swallow.

    Sancai tuhui, juan 74, p. 23

  21. 大雪 Major Snow —
    The text

    每日子丑時起身仰膝兩手左右托兩足左右踏

    In the hours of the Rat and the Ox, rise and lift the knees; both hands support left and right; tread with both feet left and right.

    Sancai tuhui, juan 74, p. 24

  22. 冬至 Winter Solstice 3–5
    The text

    每日子丑時平坐伸兩足拳兩手按兩膝左右極力三五度吐納叩齒咽液

    Sit level and extend both legs. Clench both hands into fists and press them on both knees, left and right, with all your strength, three to five times. Breathe; click the teeth; swallow.

    Sancai tuhui, juan 74, p. 25

  23. 小寒 Minor Cold 3–5
    The text

    每日子丑時正坐一手按足一手上托挽手互換極力三五度吐納叩齒漱咽

    Sit upright. Press one hand on the foot while the other reaches and pulls upward; exchange hands, with all your strength, three to five times. Breathe; click the teeth; rinse and swallow.

    Sancai tuhui, juan 74, p. 26

  24. 大寒 Major Cold 3–5
    The text

    每日子丑時兩手踞牀跪坐一足直伸一足用力左右三五度叩齒漱咽吐納

    Squat on the bed with both hands supporting. Kneel and sit; stretch one leg straight while the other applies force; left and right, three to five times. Click the teeth; rinse and swallow; breathe.

    Sancai tuhui, juan 74, p. 27

The Eight Brocades 八段錦

Same chapter, the method pages that follow the year

After the year, the chapter prints the eight methods that the seasonal exercises draw on, each with its own woodcut. This is the seated Eight Brocades as printed in 1609.

36

叩齒集神 Click the teeth, gather the spirit

叩齒集神三十六，兩手抱崑崙。右法先須閉目冥心，盤坐握固，靜思然後叩齒集神。次又兩手向項後，數九息，勿令耳聞。乃後手各掩耳，以第二指壓中指，擊彈腦後，左右各二十四次。

Click the teeth to gather the spirit thirty-six times. Both hands embrace Kunlun. First close the eyes and quiet the mind; sit cross-legged with the hands in the firm grip; meditate in silence, then click the teeth. Then take both hands behind the neck and count nine breaths, so quietly your ears cannot hear them. Then cover each ear with a hand, press the index finger over the middle finger, and snap it against the back of the skull, twenty-four times on each side.

Kunlun, the sacred mountain, is the head. The “firm grip” tucks the thumb inside the fist.

Sancai tuhui, juan 74, p. 28

24

搖天柱 Shake the Heavenly Pillar

左右手搖天柱各二十四。右法先須握固，乃搖頭左右顧，肩膊隨動二十四。

Shake the Heavenly Pillar left and right, twenty-four times each. First the firm grip; then shake the head, looking left and right, the shoulders moving with it, twenty-four times.

The Heavenly Pillar is the neck.

Sancai tuhui, juan 74, p. 29

36 · 36 · 3

舌攪漱咽 Stir the tongue, rinse, swallow

左右舌攪上腭三十六，漱三十六，分作三口，如硬物嚥之，然後方得行火。右法以舌攪口齒并左右頰，待津液生，方漱之，至滿口方嚥之。

Stir the tongue against the upper palate thirty-six times, left and right. Rinse thirty-six times. Divide the fluid into three mouthfuls and swallow each as if it were something solid. Only then may the fire be circulated. Stir the tongue over teeth and cheeks until the fluid rises, rinse it, and swallow only when the mouth is full.

Sancai tuhui, juan 74, p. 30

36

摩腎堂 Rub the Kidney Hall

兩手摩腎堂三十六，以數多更妙。右法閉氣搓手令熱，後摩腎堂如數畢，仍収手握固，再閉氣，想用心火下燒丹田，覺熱極即止。

Rub the Kidney Hall with both hands thirty-six times; more is better still. Hold the breath and rub the hands together until hot, then rub the Kidney Hall the full count. Withdraw the hands into the firm grip, hold the breath again, and imagine the heart’s fire burning down into the cinnabar field. Stop when the heat is at its height.

The Kidney Hall is the small of the back.

Sancai tuhui, juan 74, p. 31

36 + 36

單關轆轤 The single windlass

左右單關轆轤三十六。右法須俯首擺撼左肩三十六次，右肩亦三十六次。

The single windlass, left and right, thirty-six. Lower the head and sway the left shoulder thirty-six times; then the right shoulder, also thirty-six.

A windlass cranks: the shoulder rolls to pump the breath up the spine.

Sancai tuhui, juan 74, p. 32

36

雙關轆轤 The double windlass

雙關轆轤三十六。右法兩肩並擺撼至三十六數，想火自丹田透雙關入腦戶，鼻引清氣，後伸兩脚。

The double windlass, thirty-six. Sway both shoulders together to the count of thirty-six; imagine fire from the cinnabar field passing through the double gate and entering the brain chamber. Draw clear breath in through the nose, then stretch out both legs.

Sancai tuhui, juan 74, p. 33

5 · 9 · 3 or 9

托天按頂 Support heaven, press the crown

兩手相搓當呵五呵，後叉手托天按頂各九次。右法叉手相交，向上托空三次或九次。

Rub the hands together and make the “he” sound five times; then interlace the hands, support heaven and press the crown, nine times each. Interlace the fingers and push up into empty space, three times or nine.

“He” is a breathed-out sound made without the voice.

Sancai tuhui, juan 74, p. 34

12 · 24

鈎攀 Hook and pull

以兩手如鈎向前攀雙脚心十二，再収足端坐，轆轤二十四次，想丹田火自下而上遍燒身體，想時口鼻皆須閉氣少頃。

With both hands hooked, reach forward and pull the soles of both feet twelve times. Draw the feet back and sit upright; windlass twenty-four times, imagining the fire of the cinnabar field rising from below to burn through the whole body. While imagining, close off mouth and nose and hold the breath a moment.

Sancai tuhui, juan 74, p. 35

The Five Animal Frolics 五禽戲

Hua Tuo, 2nd century, as preserved in Essence of the Taoist Canon
7times, each animal

Hua Tuo to his disciple Wu Puc. 200

吾有一術、名曰五禽戲。一曰虎、二曰鹿、三曰熊、四曰猿、五曰鳥。⋯⋯虎戲者、四肢距地、前三擲、却二擲、長引腰、乍却仰天、即返距行前、却各七過也。鹿戲者、四肢距地、引項反顧、左三右二、左右伸脚、伸縮亦三亦二也。熊戲者、正仰、以兩手抱膝下、舉頭、左僻地七、右亦七。⋯⋯猿戲者、攀物自懸、伸縮身體、上下一七。⋯⋯鳥戲者、雙立手、翹一足、伸兩臂、揚眉鼓力、右二七。

“I have a method called the Five Animal Frolics: first the tiger, second the deer, third the bear, fourth the ape, fifth the bird. … The tiger: all four limbs on the ground, spring forward three times and back two, stretch the waist long, then turn the face to the sky, return to all fours and go forward and back, seven times each. The deer: four limbs on the ground, stretch the neck and look back, three to the left and two to the right, and stretch the legs out to left and right, three and two. The bear: lie on the back, hold below the knees with both hands, lift the head, and drop to the ground seven times on the left and seven on the right. … The ape: hang from something, stretch and contract the body, up and down seven times. … The bird: stand with the hands together, lift one foot, spread both arms, raise the brows and gather strength, twice seven on the right.”

“Do it until you sweat, then stop, and dust the body with powder.” Wu Pu, the text says, practised it past ninety with his teeth intact.

Essence of the Taoist Canon, p. 151

Holding the breath 胎息

Ge Hong, Baopuzi, inner chapters · c. 320
120counts, rising to a thousand

Embryonic breathingJin dynasty

初學行炁，鼻中引炁而閉之，陰以心數至一百二十，乃以口微吐之。及引之，皆不欲令己耳聞其出入之聲，常令入多出少。以鴻毛著鼻口之上，吐炁而鴻毛不動為候也。漸自轉增其心數，久可以至千。

“When first learning to circulate the breath, draw it in through the nose and hold it. Silently, in the heart, count to one hundred and twenty; then let it out gently through the mouth. Neither the drawing in nor the letting out should be loud enough for your own ears to hear. Always let more come in than goes out. Lay a goose-down feather over the nose and mouth: when you breathe out and the feather does not move, you have it. Gradually increase the count. In time you can reach a thousand.”

Baopuzi, inner chapters, folio 7, pp. 23–24

The seat आसन

Svātmārāma, Haṭhayogapradīpikā, with the commentary and a Hindi gloss · text c. 1450

The Haṭhayogapradīpikā names eighty-four postures and describes four seats. The commentary specifies the placement: which heel, which side, how many fingers between chin and chest. Root verse, then commentary, then the Hindi vernacular gloss, all on one printed page.

4fingers, chin to chest

Siddhāsana, the adept’s seatverse I.35

योनिस्थानकमंघ्रिमूलघटितं कृत्वा दृढं विन्यसेन्मेंढ्रे पादमथैकमेव हृदये कृत्वा हनुं सुस्थिरम् ॥ स्थाणुः संयमितेन्द्रियोऽचलदृशा पश्येद्भ्रुवोरंतरं ह्येतन्मोक्षकपाटभेदजनकं सिद्धासनं प्रोच्यते ॥ ३५ ॥

“Press the heel firmly against the perineum. Place the other foot above the genitals. Fix the chin firmly against the heart. Remaining steady with the senses controlled and a steady gaze, look at the space between the eyebrows. This is called the adept’s seat; it forces open the door to liberation.”

अंघ्रिर्वामश्चरणस्तस्य मूलेन पार्ष्णिभागेन घटितं संलग्नं कृत्वा । स्थानांन्तरं एकं पादं दक्षिणं पादं मेंढ्रैंद्रियस्योपरिभागे दृढं यथा स्यात्तथा विन्यसेत् । हृदये हृदयसमीपे हनुं चिबुकं सुस्थिरं सम्यक्स्थिरं कृत्वा हनुहृदययोश्चतुरंगुलमंतरं यथा भवति तथा कृत्वेति रहस्यं ।

The commentary: “Having placed the base of the left foot, meaning the heel, firmly against the perineum, one should then place the other foot, the right, firmly on the upper part of the genitals. Fix the chin steadily near the heart, so that there is a gap of four fingers between chin and chest. That is the secret.”

The next verse gives the other school’s version, left ankle above the genitals, right ankle on top, and lists the pose’s other names: vajrāsana, muktāsana, guptāsana.

Haṭhayogapradīpikā with commentaries, pp. 34–35

Bhedanāsana, the piercing posture, in Hindi verseSvarodaya, c. 1800

भेदन आसन कह्यो बुझाई प्रथम दृजानू बैठ कथा ई ॥५३॥ दोहा मुख वाम करा बांध के दाहिन जाम परथाप दक्षिण कुदनी तास पर धरै कछुकत हो चाप ॥५४॥ चौपई पुन कर दाहिन मुही बंधावै ठोड़ी ति लें सहत बल कावै युगुत चतुर कर कटि न कराई नाभी औ च पीठ सो लाई ॥५५॥

“The piercing posture, explained: first sit on both knees. Bind the left hand near the face and place it on the right thigh; set the right heel against the body and press a little. Then bind the right hand the same way and hold the chin with steady strength. The clever practitioner does not let the waist bend, and draws the navel toward the spine.”

Braj Bhasha verse, in the dohā and chaupāī metres, printed around 1800. The heel is kudanī; the couplet numbers are the poem’s own.

Discourse on the Rising of the Breath (Svarodaya), p. 17

The eight retentions अष्टकुम्भक

Haṭhayogapradīpikā II.44–67, Sanskrit edition of 1867

Prāṇāyāma in haṭha yoga is kumbhaka, the held breath, and there are eight named kinds. The text gives the method for each in a verse or two: which nostril, what sound, how far to fill, when to stop.

8named retentions

The listII.44

सूर्यभेदनमुज्जायी सीत्कारी शीतली तथा । भस्त्रिका भ्रामरी मूर्च्छा प्लाविनीत्यष्टकुम्भकाः ॥ ४४ ॥

“Sun-piercing, victorious, hissing, cooling, bellows, bee, swooning, floating: these are the eight retentions.”

Haṭhayogapradīpikā, 1867, p. 79

to the limit

Sūryabhedana, sun-piercingII.48–50

आसने सुखदे योगी बद्ध्वा चैवासनं ततः । दक्षनाड्या समाकृष्य बहिःस्थं पवनं शनैः ॥ ४८ ॥ आकेशादानखाग्राच्च निरोधावधि कुंभयेत् । ततः शनैः सव्यनाड्या रेचयेत्पवनं शनैः ॥ ४९ ॥ कपालशोधनं वातदोषघ्नं कृमिदोषहृत् । पुनः पुनरिदं कार्यं सूर्यभेदनमुत्तमम् ॥ ५० ॥

“Seated comfortably in his posture, the yogi should slowly draw the outer air in through the right channel. He should hold it to the limit of retention, from the hair to the tips of the nails. Then slowly, slowly, let the breath out through the left channel. It cleanses the skull, destroys the disorders of wind, and removes worms. Do this excellent sun-piercing again and again.”

Haṭhayogapradīpikā, 1867, pp. 81–84

Ujjāyī, the victoriousII.51–53

The Platonists ἄσκησις

Greek and Latin · the Hermetica, the Pythagorean life, the magical papyri, Proclus, Plethon, Ficino

The late antique philosophical schools taught a practice as well as a doctrine. Their texts give the hour, the direction, the posture, the breath and the count, but inside dialogues, biographies and liturgies rather than in manuals. The line runs from the Hermetica and Iamblichus through Proclus to the Byzantine Plethon and to Ficino, who translated Plato, Plotinus and the Hermetica into Latin and wrote the same kind of instruction into his regimen for scholars.

“For it is fitting for you also, when praying under the open sky, to turn your face to the south as the sun sets, and at sunrise to the east wind.”

Hermes gives his son Tat the posture before he sings the hymn: outdoors, facing a fixed direction for each hour. Ficino’s abbreviations are expanded.

The Haṭhayogapradīpikā names eighty-four āsanas and draws none. The Śrītattvanidhi, compiled at the Mysore court around 1800, draws a hundred and twenty-two, the earliest illustrated āsana series. The library holds the plates below.

The Chinese instructions are the text as printed; a few characters on worn leaves are marked. Translations are machine-assisted from the scans, so read the page before relying on a phrase.

Where it comes from

The year and the brocades: Sancai tuhui, the illustrated encyclopedia of 1609, juan 74. The animals and the breath count: Essence of the Taoist Canon (1922 collection) and Ge Hong’s Baopuzi (c. 320). The seat: the Haṭhayogapradīpikā printed with its commentary and a Hindi gloss. The eight retentions: the Sanskrit edition of 1867. The measured breath: a Sanskrit leaf preserved at Gangtey, Bhutan. The plates: the Śrītattvanidhi (Mysore, c. 1800), a Nyang-tradition Tibetan manuscript, the 1922 Marathi Mallakhamb manual and a 1927 photograph. The Platonists: Ficino’s Latin Pimander (1481), Iamblichus ed. Nauck (1884), the Greek Magical Papyri ed. Preisendanz (1928), Marinus’ Life of Proclus (1814), Plethon’s Laws (1858) and Ficino’s De vita (1489). The rites: the Latin and English Keys of Solomon, the Rituale Romanum of 1615, and the Ars Notoria of 1657. Elsewhere: the Greek Philokalia of 1893, an Arabic Iḥyāʾ, Cassian in the 1872 French, the Missale Romanum, Mercuriale 1573, Santorio 1614, Thibault 1628 and the Mānasollāsa.

What is still closed

Recently transcribed. Chao Yuanfang’s Zhubing yuanhou lun (610), the oldest body of daoyin prescriptions we hold, is now transcribed and translated in all nine volumes instead of its first leaves only; so is the exercise volume of Gao Lian’s Zunsheng bajian (1591), Sun Simiao’s chapters on nourishing life, and the 1922 Marathi Mallakhamb manual. Ignatius’ Exercitia spiritualia is now transcribed. Abulafia’s complete writings are transcribed (2,703 of 2,707 pages) and translated. Arbeau’s Orchésographie, Marozzo, Fabris and the Talhoffer facsimile were acquired for this page and are now readable too.

Still closed. The Yijin jing, source of most later qigong sets, is not held. Caroso and Negri have no usable scan we can find. The Hesychast breath-prayer — chin on the chest, gaze at the navel — should be in our Greek Philokalia of 1893 and is not on any transcribed page; what is there is the one sentence from Hesychios quoted above. And the volume of al-Ghazālī’s Iḥyāʾ that carries the prayer instructions is a printing we cannot publish.
